core_summary: This chapter introduces the fundamental concepts of chemical reactions, symbolic representation via word and balanced chemical equations, and the law of conservation of mass. It details five primary types of chemical reactions: combination, decomposition, displacement, double displacement, and oxidation-reduction (redox) reactions. It also explores practical manifestations of redox reactions in everyday life, namely corrosion of metals and rancidity of fats and oils.
key_concepts: Symbolic representation of chemical changes through word equations and chemical equations
Law of Conservation of Mass requiring equal atom counts of each element on reactant and product sides
Combination reactions where two or more reactants unite to form a single product
Decomposition reactions driven by thermal, electrolytic, or photolytic energy inputs
Displacement reactions where a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its salt solution
Double displacement reactions involving mutual exchange of ions between two aqueous compounds forming a precipitate
Exothermic reactions releasing heat energy versus endothermic reactions absorbing energy
Oxidation as oxygen gain/hydrogen loss and Reduction as oxygen loss/hydrogen gain occurring simultaneously in redox reactions
Corrosion as environmental degradation of metals and Rancidity as oxidation of fats/oils causing spoiled taste and odor

key_terms.definition: Substances that undergo chemical change during a chemical reaction, written on the left-hand side of an equation.
New substances formed during a chemical reaction, written on the right-hand side of an equation.
An unbalanced chemical equation that represents the chemical formula of reactants and products without balancing mass.
A reaction in which two or more reactants combine to form a single product.
A reaction in which a single reactant breaks down into two or more simpler products.
A chemical reaction accompanied by the release of heat energy to the surroundings.
A chemical reaction that absorbs energy in the form of heat, light, or electricity.
A reaction where a more reactive element replaces a less reactive element in a compound.
A reaction involving an exchange of ions between two reactant compounds to produce new compounds.
An insoluble solid product formed during an aqueous chemical reaction.
A chemical process involving the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen by a substance.
A chemical process involving the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen by a substance.
A chemical reaction in which oxidation and reduction occur simultaneously.
The slow eating away of metals by the action of air, moisture, or chemicals on their surface.
The unpleasant alteration of odor and taste in fats and oils caused by aerial oxidation.

key_takeaways: Chemical equations must always be balanced to conform to the law of conservation of mass.
Physical state symbols (s, l, g, aq) and specific reaction conditions provide complete quantitative and structural context for chemical reactions.
Decomposition reactions are thermo-chemically opposite to combination reactions.
In displacement reactions, reactivity series determines whether one metal can displace another from its compound.
Antioxidants and nitrogen flushing effectively prevent food rancidity by inhibiting oxidation.
